summary: All days of the week are masculine (der Montag … der Sonntag; der Mittwoch too), and so are the parts of the day except die Nacht. On a day, a part of the day or the weekend German uses am (an + dem): am Montag, am Morgen, am Mittag, am Nachmittag, am Abend, am Wochenende – but in der Nacht. A habit – every Monday, every morning – is an adverb with -s, written small: montags, morgens, mittags, abends, nachts. With heute, morgen and gestern the part of the day follows: heute Abend, gestern Morgen – but tomorrow morning is morgen früh. Do not confuse morgen (tomorrow, small m) and der Morgen (the morning, capital M). You say the day with sein: Heute ist Montag. Gestern war Sonntag (war = was). Welcher Tag ist heute? A time word very often opens the sentence; then the verb comes second and the subject follows it: Am Montag gehe ich zur Arbeit. Morgen fahren wir nach Berlin. Inside the sentence, time comes before manner and place: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Bus nach Berlin. German uses the present tense for the future when a time word is there: Morgen komme ich zurück. How often: immer (always), oft (often), manchmal (sometimes), nie (never) – after the verb: Wir essen oft Fisch. jetzt (now), später (later), bald (soon), früh (early), spät (late): Ich gehe jetzt. Wir essen später. Er kommt immer spät nach Hause.

blocks.caption: How often – from always to never
A time word first: the verb stays second, the subject moves behind it

blocks.title: morgen – der Morgen
blocks.text: morgen = tomorrow; der Morgen = the morning; morgens = in the mornings. Tomorrow morning = morgen früh (not *morgen Morgen).

blocks.title: Not *Am Montag ich gehe
blocks.text: German keeps the verb in second place: Am Montag gehe ich … · Heute ist … · Manchmal fahre ich …

blocks.title: Tonight
blocks.text: heute Abend = this evening / tonight (going out); heute Nacht = tonight in bed – or last night.

items.title: German
points: names after the moon, gods and the sun: Montag (moon day), Donnerstag (Donar’s day), Sonntag (sun day)
Mittwoch = mid-week; the week starts on Monday

items.title: Arabic, Hebrew, Chinese
points: numbered days: Hebrew יוֹם שֵׁנִי (second day), Arabic الاثْنَيْن (from “two”), Chinese 星期一 (week-one) – all three are Monday
Arabic and Hebrew count from Sunday, Chinese from Monday

askYourself: A day, a part of the day or the weekend? → am (am Montag, am Abend, am Wochenende).
The night? → in der Nacht (or nachts).
Every week, every morning – a habit? → montags, morgens, abends (small letter, -s).
today / yesterday / tomorrow + part of the day? → heute Abend, gestern Morgen; tomorrow morning = morgen früh.
Is it morgen (tomorrow) or der Morgen (the morning)?
Does the time word open the sentence? → the verb comes next, the subject after it.
Several pieces in the middle? → time – manner – place: morgen – mit dem Bus – nach Berlin.
Future meaning? → present tense + a time word.
How often? → immer, oft, manchmal, nie – after the verb.
steps: Put it first or after the verb – the verb stays second.

traps: montags, morgens, abends are written small; Montag, Morgen, Abend capital.
Am Montag gehe ich … – not *Am Montag ich gehe …
Days and parts of the day are masculine: der Montag, der Abend, der Mittwoch (die Woche, but der Mittwoch).
gestern needs the past: Gestern war Sonntag (war = was, the past of ist).

quiz.q: On Monday I go to work.
options: Am Montag gehe ich zur Arbeit.
Am Montag ich gehe zur Arbeit.
In Montag gehe ich zur Arbeit.
quiz.answer: Am Montag gehe ich zur Arbeit.
quiz.why: am + day; the verb stays in second place.
The night is the exception: in der Nacht.
All weekdays are masculine – Mittwoch too.
heute + part of the day with a capital: heute Abend.
The frequency adverb follows the verb.

seeAlso.note: Arabic numbers most days: الأَحَد (“one”, Sunday), الاثْنَيْن (“two”, Monday) … الخَمِيس (“five”, Thursday); الجُمُعَة is “the gathering”, السَّبْت “the Sabbath”; “on Monday” is يَوْمَ الاثْنَيْنِ.
Hebrew numbers the days too: יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן (Sunday, “first day”) … יוֹם שִׁשִּׁי, then שַׁבָּת; “on Monday” = בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי.
Chinese numbers the weekdays (星期一 … 星期六, 星期天) and puts the time word before the verb (我星期一去上班) – no preposition, no verb-second rule.
Chinese marks finished actions with 了 / 过; German uses the past tense (war) – the full past comes after the foundations.
am Montag, im Mai, um acht Uhr: the prepositions of time follow in the next step.

notes.text: Greek uses no preposition (τη Δευτέρα, το πρωί, το βράδυ); German needs am: am Montag, am Morgen, am Abend – but in der Nacht. Greek numbers the days (Δευτέρα = second, Τρίτη = third), German names them (Montag = moon day).

в понедельник is am Montag; среда and Mittwoch both mean “middle”, while вторник, четверг, пятница are numbered. A time word first pulls the German verb before the subject: Am Montag gehe ich …, not *Am Montag ich gehe.
lunes (moon) is Montag, and el lunes / los lunes match am Montag / montags; German adds verb-second: Am Montag arbeite ich.

Monday, Thursday, Friday, Sunday share their origin with Montag, Donnerstag, Freitag, Sonntag. on Monday – am Montag; on Mondays – montags. After a time word German puts the verb before the subject: Heute koche ich.
lundi (moon) is Montag; le lundi (every Monday) is montags. After a time word German puts the verb before the subject: Am Montag gehe ich …
somvār (moon day) and ravivār (sun day) follow the same planetary week as Montag and Sonntag.
Persian counts from Saturday (šanbe, yekšanbe, došanbe = Monday); German names the days after the moon, gods and the sun.
somvār (moon day) and ravivār (sun day): the same planetary week as Montag and Sonntag.
Arabic numbers the days from Sunday (al-aḥad, al-ithnayn …), and Friday is al-jumuʿa (the gathering); German names them after the moon, gods and the sun, and the week starts on Monday.
Hebrew numbers the days from Sunday (yom rishon, yom sheni …) up to Shabbat; German names them, and the week starts on Monday.
Turkish uses günü or nothing for a day (pazartesi günü) and -leri for a habit (pazartesileri); German says am Montag and montags, and puts the verb second after the time word.
getsuyōbi (moon day) and nichiyōbi (sun day) match Montag and Sonntag; German adds am and verb-second: Am Montag arbeite ich.
woryoil (moon day) and iryoil (sun day) match Montag and Sonntag; German adds am and verb-second.
keskiviikko (“mid-week”) is Mittwoch, and the essive -na marks the day (maanantaina = am Montag); German uses a preposition and puts the verb second after it.
Hungarian marks the day with a suffix (hétfőn = am Montag) and names Monday “week-head” (hétfő); German uses am and names the days after the moon, gods and the sun.
Swahili counts from Saturday (Jumamosi, Jumapili, Jumatatu = Monday); German names the days and starts the week on Monday.
Chinese numbers the days (星期一, Monday) and needs no preposition (星期一我去上班); German says am Montag and puts the verb before the subject: Am Montag gehe ich zur Arbeit.
Vietnamese numbers the days (thứ hai = Monday, chủ nhật = Sunday); German names them, and a time word first pulls the verb before the subject.
German has a strict word-order rule that a time word triggers: whatever comes first, the conjugated verb is second (Heute koche ich). Inuktitut verbs usually come at the end, and word order is freer.
